query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In duplex and ultrafine-grained stainless steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, enhanced corrosion resistance is achieved through accelerated grain-boundary diffusion of chromium. This rapid diffusion promotes the formation and continuous self-healing of a protective Cr-rich passivating film, which reduces further corrosion in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Duplex stainless steels (e.g., DS2205) with a typical dual-phase microstructure and conventional (coarse) grain sizes.
generation.intervention: Refinement of the steel microstructure to create ultrafine-grained variants and subsequent exposure to simulated corrosive environments (such as molten salt and aqueous chloride solutions).
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under controlled temperature and chemical exposure conditions representative of those in chemical-processing and nuclear-power facilities, at temperatures where passivation via Cr enrichment is expected to be effective.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased density of grain boundaries in the ultrafine-grained steels, which facilitates enhanced diffusion of Cr atoms from the bulk to the surface.
generation.mechanism: The higher volume fraction of grain boundaries in refined steels enables faster Cr migration to the surface, leading to a more prompt and robust formation of a Cr-rich passive film. This film acts as a barrier to aggressive corrosive species, thereby reducing the overall corrosion rate compared to steels with a coarser grain structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Ultrafine-grained duplex stainless steels will display shallower chromium depletion depths and lower corrosion rates compared to their coarse-grained counterparts under identical corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained duplex stainless steels without any microstructural refinement.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid under temperatures and corrosive conditions that do not induce phase transformations or excessive dissolution, and where the Cr-based passivation is the dominant mode of corrosion protection.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative rate of chromium diffusion enhancement and the threshold conditions for optimal passivation require further detailed investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of duplex stainless steel specimens: one set with conventional coarse grains and another set processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure. Expose both sets to identical corrosive environments (e.g., molten salt and chloride-containing aqueous solutions) at controlled temperatures. Perform electrochemical testing and microscopic analyses to compare the formation and continuity of the Cr-rich passivating film in both cases.
measurements: Grain size analysis via metallography or electron microscopy
Surface and cross-sectional composition analysis (e.g., XPS/EDS) to quantify Cr enrichment in the passive film
Corrosion rate measurements via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and weight loss tests
Cr depletion depth measurements using cross-sectional analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in Cr-rich passive film formation and corrosion resistance (i.e., if corrosion rates and Cr depletion depths are comparable to or worse than those observed in coarse-grained specimens), then the hypothesis that enhanced grain-boundary diffusion of Cr drives improved corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

They contain at least four or five principal metal components and simply form a single face-centered cubic (FCC), body-centered cubic (BCC) or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase [,,,,,]. This novel concept is an important breakthrough of the past 25 years [,], as it is completely different from the traditional alloy design concepts in which one major component was selected, and other minor components were added to improve their related physical and chemical performances. It is worth mentioning that HEAs not only have simple phase structures, but also possess many excellent mechanical and physical properties, such as high tensile strength [,,], good ductility at ambient and cryogenic temperatures [,], superior wear and fatigue resistance [], and strong radiation tolerance [,]. These unique features qualify HEAs as potential engineering materials to meet the demanding requirements for complex and harsh environment applications, particularly in the turbine, aerospace, and nuclear industries [,,,,]. cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
